name: One Relative Section Suffices for Mixed-Puncture Retention
statement: Let an ample family $H$ contain a marked edge with endpoints $a_0,a_1$, and write $A_0,A_1$ for its sections, $D=A_0\cap A_1$, and $C=A_0\cup A_1$. Replace the edge coordinate by a binary block, with root square $T$. If at least one section peels relatively to $D$, then for either mixed word $q$, the block replacement peels to $T\setminus\{q\}$ exactly when $H$ peels to each marked endpoint. The forward implication holds without the relative-section hypothesis. Therefore any counterexample to the reverse implication without that hypothesis must have both relative sections fail, and each exclusive wing must contain a cyclic component of at least nine vertices.
proof: Reducing any proposed block peeling in each new coordinate and deleting repetitions produces rooted peelings of $H$ to both endpoints, proving necessity. For sufficiency, normalize so $A_0$ peels to $D$. Delete its exclusive wing in one nonconstant block row. The absence of edges between opposite exclusive wings makes every lifted deletion valid. One retained block section is now a copy of $H$ and the other is a peripheral family containing it; use the two endpoint orders to delete the copy and then the smaller retained row, followed by the contraction order for $C$. Exactly the three unpunctured root-square vertices remain. If both relative sections fail, the component-expansion theorem says each overlap-plus-component family is ample; the relative forest and eight-facet theorem would peel a wing whose components were all trees or had at most eight vertices, yielding the final necessary condition.
comments: The relative hypothesis is sufficient and is not claimed necessary. The theorem gives no endpoint-only converse when both sections fail.
